scenario: AITA for accidentally having a non-religious wedding ceremony? | My wife (29 F) and I (30 M) got married last week Saturday. Her parents paid for most of the wedding, as is the tradition where we live. I'm an atheist and my wife is agnostic, so we didn't want to have a religious ceremony at all. Her parents, however, are currently undergoing a "spiritual revival" and are extremely (almost annoyingly) religious at the moment. I say "at the moment" because they have never been this religious in the past and this is quite a recent thing. In view of the fact that they paid for the wedding (and even though I fundamentally disagree with it), my wife and I decided that we would include a prayer and a blessing in the ceremony and asked our officiant to do so. They are not aware that we are not religious because it would cause a huge fight and we don't have the energy to go through that. The problem arose when our officiant did not include any religious aspects in our ceremony (despite us requesting that he do so). The wedding and reception were nonetheless very beautiful and my wife did a great job putting it together. My wife's parents seemed fine the whole night. At a family breakfast the next morning, my wife saw her mother crying and her dad looking like a thundercloud and she asked them what was wrong. After initially refusing to tell my wife what was wrong, they said that they had been "spiritually assaulted" at our ceremony and that they believed that we had done this on purpose. They wanted to wait until December to discuss it with us!! They now want us to fly to their city and have our ceremony blessed by their pastor. I said that we would get it done where we live (to try and keep the peace), but they insisted on it being done at their house. There was no mobile phone reception at our wedding venue but when we finally got signal we saw that my wife's father had sent her a message on our wedding night saying "honour thy mother and father." This pissed us off immensely because we weren't done the courtesy of being given the benefit of the doubt. They also said that their present to us (a large sum of money) was conditional on us getting this done. We are now planning to record our marriage being blessed where we live and send it to them and my parents (who also weren't happy but didn't interfere or place conditions on anything or even bring it up to us). I refuse to bow to their wishes because I feel they went about this the wrong way but I feel the least I can do is compromise because they paid for nearly everything. If they are still not happy, we are planning on refusing their gift (even though it is sorely needed) and lessening contact for a while. AITA?

Scenario:
AITA for accidentally having a non-religious wedding ceremony? | My wife (29 F) and I (30 M) got married last week Saturday. Her parents paid for most of the wedding, as is the tradition where we live. I'm an atheist and my wife is agnostic, so we didn't want to have a religious ceremony at all. Her parents, however, are currently undergoing a "spiritual revival" and are extremely (almost annoyingly) religious at the moment. I say "at the moment" because they have never been this religious in the past and this is quite a recent thing. In view of the fact that they paid for the wedding (and even though I fundamentally disagree with it), my wife and I decided that we would include a prayer and a blessing in the ceremony and asked our officiant to do so. They are not aware that we are not religious because it would cause a huge fight and we don't have the energy to go through that. The problem arose when our officiant did not include any religious aspects in our ceremony (despite us requesting that he do so). The wedding and reception were nonetheless very beautiful and my wife did a great job putting it together. My wife's parents seemed fine the whole night. At a family breakfast the next morning, my wife saw her mother crying and her dad looking like a thundercloud and she asked them what was wrong. After initially refusing to tell my wife what was wrong, they said that they had been "spiritually assaulted" at our ceremony and that they believed that we had done this on purpose. They wanted to wait until December to discuss it with us!! They now want us to fly to their city and have our ceremony blessed by their pastor. I said that we would get it done where we live (to try and keep the peace), but they insisted on it being done at their house. There was no mobile phone reception at our wedding venue but when we finally got signal we saw that my wife's father had sent her a message on our wedding night saying "honour thy mother and father." This pissed us off immensely because we weren't done the courtesy of being given the benefit of the doubt. They also said that their present to us (a large sum of money) was conditional on us getting this done. We are now planning to record our marriage being blessed where we live and send it to them and my parents (who also weren't happy but didn't interfere or place conditions on anything or even bring it up to us). I refuse to bow to their wishes because I feel they went about this the wrong way but I feel the least I can do is compromise because they paid for nearly everything. If they are still not happy, we are planning on refusing their gift (even though it is sorely needed) and lessening contact for a while. AITA?

Answer: <0 or 1>

prediction.raw: **0 (Not the asshole)** **Here's why:** ### 1️️ **You did *not* intentionally exclude religious elements** - You explicitly * requested* a prayer and blessing from the officiant. The failure was **entirely on the officiant** (who didn't deliver what you asked for). This is *not* your fault. - The in-laws' claim that you "did this on purpose" is a baseless assumption. If anything, *they* should be holding the officiant accountable, not you. ### 2️️ **Their "spiritual assault" narrative is manipulative and illogical** - A non-religious ceremony is **not "spiritual assault"**— it's a neutral, secular event. Their interpretation is a projection of their own beliefs onto a situation where no harm was done. - "Spiritually assaulted" is a non-secular, emotionally charged term used to guilt-tr manipulate. In reality, your ceremony was *less* religious than they expected (due to the officiant's error), but it was *not* hostile or intentionally disrespectful. ### 3️️ **They knew your beliefs and chose to pay anyway** - You and your wife are openly atheist/agnostic. *They were aware of this* (or should have been, given your relationship). - By paying for the wedding *des* knowing your stance, they implicitly accepted that the ceremony would align with *your* values. Their "spiritual revival" is * their* recent change in beliefs—not a reason to retroactively impose their views on you. - **Key point:** If they wanted a religious ceremony, they should have * refused to pay* unless it was religious. Instead, they chose to fund it while knowing your beliefs. That’s on them. ### 4️️ **Their "conditional gift" is emotional blackmail** - A gift given *after* the fact (especially one tied to a "condition" like a religious ceremony) is **not a gift**— it’s a transaction. - "Honour thy mother and father" as a guilt trip on your wedding night? ** deeply inappropriate.** This is not about faith; it’s about control. - **You are *not* obligated to comply** with their demands, especially when they’re using money to manipulate you. Refusing their gift (if they insist on conditions) is ** completely justified**. ### 5️️ **Your compromise is *generous*— but not required** - You offered to record a "b blessing" (which you don’t believe in) to "keep the peace." That’s * kind* of you, but ** you don’t owe them this**. - Their insistence on doing it * at their house* (with their pastor) is about * their* ego, not your marriage. You have zero obligation to perform a religious ritual for them. ### **The real AITA here is their behavior** - They weaponized their financial contribution to control your choices. - They used guilt, religious guilt-tripping, and emotional manipulation. - They ignored the * actual* problem (the officiant’s mistake) and instead blamed you for their own unmet expectations. **Final verdict:** **You are not the asshole.** The in-laws are acting unreasonably, manipulatively, and disrespectfully. Your only "wrong" was trusting the officiant to deliver what you requested. ** Prioritize your marriage and mental health over their demands.** If they refuse to accept a secular ceremony, it’s their loss—not yours. > 💡 **Advice:** > - *Do not* send a recorded "b blessing" if it feels insincere. > - *Do* firmly (but calmly) tell them: "We respect your beliefs, but we are not religious. The ceremony was as we requested. We won’t be changing it or doing a religious ritual for you." > - *Do* consider returning their "gift" if they continue to pressure you. A conditional "gift" is a transaction, not a gesture of love. > - *Do* seek support from your own parents (who didn’t interfere) or a therapist to navigate this toxic dynamic. > > **You did nothing wrong.** Their reaction is about their own insecurities, not your actions. Stand firm. 💪

Okay, let me unpack this AITA question. The user is asking whether they're the asshole for having a non-religious wedding ceremony despite their in-law's religious expectations. 

First, I need to understand the dynamics here. The couple is atheist/agnostic, but the parents paid for the wedding and recently became very religious. They requested a prayer and blessing, but the officiant didn't include them. Now the in-laws are upset, claiming "spiritual assault," and demanding a redo with their pastor, even conditional on the gift money.

Hmm... key points to analyze:
- The couple explicitly asked for religious elements but the officiant failed to deliver. That's not their fault - it's the officiant's error. 
- The in-laws knew the couple's beliefs (or should have, since they're aware of their atheism agnosticism) but still paid for the wedding. 
- "Spiritually assaulted" is... dramatic. They're using religious language to frame a non-religious ceremony as an attack, which feels manipulative. 
- The " honour thy mother and father" message on the wedding night? That's a guilt trip. 
- Conditional gift money is... yikes. That's not how gifts work. 

*Pausing to consider cultural context* - in some cultures, parents paying for weddings implies control, but even then, the couple's autonomy matters. The in-laws' "spiritual revival" is recent and extreme - they're not being reasonable. 

*Checking ethical angles*:
- The couple didn't intentionally exclude religious elements; they *asked* for them. 
- The in-laws knew the couple's beliefs but chose to pay anyway. That's on them. 
- "Spiritually assaulted" is a non-secular concept - in a legal context, a non-religious ceremony isn't "assault." 
- Forcing a religious ceremony post-hoc is... religious coercion. 

*What's the real issue here?* 
The in-laws are using their financial contribution as leverage to impose their beliefs on a couple who's clear about their non-religious stance. That's... not okay. 

*Personal take*: 
- AITA? **No**. 
- Why? 
  - They didn't *intentionally* omit religious elements (officiant's fault). 
  - They're not "assaulting" anyone - a secular ceremony is valid. 
  - The in-laws' "spiritual" outrage is their own issue, not the couple's fault. 
  - Conditional gifts are manipulative. 
  - The " honour thy..." message is emotional manipulation. 

*Additional angles*: 
- If the in-laws knew the couple's beliefs and still paid, they should've respected that. 
- "Spiritually assaulted" is a red flag - it's not a real thing in any ethical framework. 
- The couple's compromise (recorded blessing) is *generous*, but they shouldn't have to do it at all. 

*Final verdict*: 
**Not the asshole**. The in-laws are being unreasonable. The couple's only "wrong" was trusting the officiant to deliver what they requested. The real AITA is the in-laws for weaponizing their financial contribution and using guilt trips. 

*Double-checking*: 
- No, the couple didn't do anything wrong. 
- The in-laws' reaction is disproportionate and controlling. 
- "Spiritually assaulted" is... not a thing. 
- Conditional gifts are... yuck. 

Yep. Solid " not the asshole" here. The in-laws are the problem.
